practice.stem: Which neurotransmitter is released by ALL autonomic preganglionic neurons?
options: Acetylcholine in the PNS, norepinephrine in the SNS
practice.rationale: "It's always acetylcholine from that first neuron" — both divisions release ACh onto Nn receptors at the ganglion. Norepinephrine is the SNS postganglionic transmitter, and epinephrine comes from the adrenal medulla.

practice.stem: Which receptor is found at the skeletal muscle neuromuscular junction?
practice.rationale: N for nerve, M for muscle: Nm sits at the NMJ. Nn is at the autonomic ganglia; muscarinic receptors are on PNS target organs and sweat glands; α₁ is on smooth muscle.

practice.stem: Activation of α₂ receptors produces:
options: Decreased NE release and sympathetic outflow
practice.rationale: α₂ is the sympathetic system's negative feedback — "the brother that's always like, no, don't." Vasoconstriction is α₁, ↑ HR/contractility is β₁, bronchodilation is β₂.

practice.stem: Positive dromotropy from β₁ stimulation means:
options: Increased renin release from the kidney
Faster conduction through the AV junction
Faster heart rate from the SA node
practice.rationale: Dromotropy = conduction. Chronotropy (chrono = time) is rate, and inotropy is strength of contraction. Renin release is β₁'s kidney effect.

practice.stem: Sweat glands are the exception in autonomic wiring because they are:
options: Sympathetic, using norepinephrine at α₁ receptors
Sympathetic, but use ACh at muscarinic receptors
Parasympathetic, using ACh at muscarinic receptors
Innervated equally by both autonomic divisions
practice.rationale: Sweat glands are sympathetic, but the nerve releases ACh onto muscarinic receptors, so with drugs "sweating will follow the opposite of what you expect." The PNS has no significant sweat-gland innervation.

practice.stem: Which structure is innervated by only ONE division of the ANS?
practice.rationale: Blood vessels get essentially no parasympathetic input — "it's all sympathetic." The heart, bladder and eye have dual, opposed innervation.

practice.stem: Bethanechol's main therapeutic use is:
options: Urinary retention caused by an enlarged prostate
practice.rationale: Bethanechol makes the detrusor contract, so it's for a bladder that holds urine but can't contract — never when there's an obstruction. Atropine treats bradycardia; pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.

practice.stem: Pyridostigmine is used to treat:
practice.rationale: Pyridostigmine (AChE inhibitor) keeps more ACh at the NMJ for myasthenia gravis. Neostigmine is the one that reverses nondepolarizing blockade; atropine treats cholinergic toxicity; dantrolene treats MH.

practice.stem: What is the antidote for malignant hyperthermia?
practice.rationale: Dantrolene is the MH antidote and must be rapidly available wherever triggering agents are used. Atropine treats cholinergic toxicity; neostigmine and pyridostigmine are AChE inhibitors.

practice.stem: Which is an EARLY clue of malignant hyperthermia?
practice.rationale: CO₂ reflects metabolism, so rising end-tidal CO₂ is "often the first sign"; hyperthermia may be a late sign. MH brings tachycardia and rigidity, not bradycardia or flaccidity.

practice.stem: Which drugs are nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers?
practice.rationale: Nondepolarizers "end in -curonium" and are Nm antagonists. Succinylcholine is the depolarizing agent; neostigmine and pyridostigmine are AChE inhibitors; bethanechol and atropine act at muscarinic receptors.

practice.stem: Clonidine (Catapres) is classified as a:
practice.rationale: Clonidine stimulates central presynaptic α₂ receptors to cut NE release. Prazosin is the α₁ antagonist, metoprolol the β₁-selective blocker, phenylephrine the selective α₁ agonist.

practice.stem: Which β-blocker is cardioselective (preferentially blocks β₁)?
practice.rationale: Metoprolol preferentially blocks β₁. Propranolol blocks β₁ + β₂, carvedilol blocks β₁ + β₂ + α₁, and prazosin isn't a β-blocker (α₁ antagonist).

practice.stem: Botulinum toxin works by:
options: Blocking Nm receptors at the NMJ
practice.rationale: Botulinum toxin acts at the presynaptic terminal so ACh never reaches the receptor. Blocking Nm is rocuronium/vecuronium; AChE inhibition is pyridostigmine/neostigmine; muscarinic activation is bethanechol.

practice.stem: An α₁ agonist causes vasoconstriction. What happens to blood pressure if a patient receives an α₁ antagonist?
options: BP falls because heart rate drops through β₁ blockade
BP is unchanged because the parasympathetic system takes over the vessels
practice.rationale: Blocking α₁ removes the signal to constrict, so vessels dilate and BP falls. Vessels have no parasympathetic input to "take over," and an α₁ blocker doesn't act on β₁.

practice.stem: A patient with urinary retention has a bethanechol order. Which finding should make the nurse hold the dose and contact the prescriber?
options: No void for 8 hours after surgery
A bladder scan showing a large volume of urine
A kidney stone lodged in the urethra
practice.rationale: "Make sure there's a place for the urine to go" — squeezing a bladder against an obstruction can rupture it. A full bladder and no void are why the drug is ordered; normal vitals aren't a reason to hold it.

practice.stem: A patient received atropine. Which assessment finding is an expected drug effect?
practice.rationale: Atropine = dry + fast + retention: tachycardia, dry mouth, mydriasis, constipation. Bradycardia, salivation, diarrhea and miosis are cholinergic effects — the opposite.

practice.stem: An 84-year-old taking several medications with anticholinergic properties becomes newly confused. The most likely explanation is:
practice.rationale: Older adults are "much more sensitive" to anticholinergics and the effects add up across drugs; confusion/agitation is a listed CNS effect. Cholinergic toxicity would bring SLUDGE signs instead.

practice.stem: A patient on pyridostigmine develops muscle twitching, drooling and diarrhea. The nurse suspects:
practice.rationale: Fasciculations ("twitches") plus salivation and diarrhea = too much ACh — "it may mean that we've given them too much." Anticholinergic toxicity would be dry, constipated and retaining.

practice.stem: Which drug should the nurse anticipate to treat dangerous muscarinic effects of cholinergic toxicity?
practice.rationale: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and is used to treat cholinergic toxicity. Neostigmine and bethanechol would add more cholinergic activity; dantrolene is for MH.

practice.stem: A ventilated ICU patient is receiving vecuronium and lies completely still. Which action is a priority?
options: Stop respiratory support as soon as the infusion is turned off
Skip eye care because the patient's eyes are closed by the drug
Confirm that sedation and analgesia are also being given
Decrease sedation because the paralytic keeps the patient calm
practice.rationale: PARALYSIS ≠ SEDATION ≠ ANALGESIA — a paralyzed patient can be awake and in pain. Paralyzed patients need eye/skin care, and recovery must be verified before respiratory support stops.

practice.stem: A patient on rocuronium is also started on gentamicin. What interaction should the nurse watch for?
practice.rationale: Aminoglycosides like gentamicin (along with general anesthetics and magnesium) can increase or prolong nondepolarizing blockade. MH and sux-type hyperkalemia belong to succinylcholine.

practice.stem: Why does neostigmine reverse rocuronium?
options: It blocks the muscarinic receptors instead
More ACh outcompetes the blocker at Nm
It speeds the breakdown of rocuronium
It directly stimulates the Nm receptors
practice.rationale: Neostigmine inhibits AChE, so ACh builds up and outcompetes the nondepolarizing blocker. It doesn't activate the receptor itself, and the muscarinic effects it causes are why an antimuscarinic is often given with it.

practice.stem: A patient with major burns from 3 weeks ago needs emergent intubation. Why is succinylcholine a concern?
options: Burns trigger malignant hyperthermia by themselves
Upregulated receptors → severe hyperkalemia and dysrhythmias
Burns make the patient resistant to all paralytics
Succinylcholine causes hypokalemia in burn patients
practice.rationale: After the acute phase, burns upregulate extrajunctional receptors — more channels open, more K⁺ leaves muscle, "their bodies are a little more primed." MH is genetic, triggered by sux or volatile anesthetics, not by burns.

practice.stem: After surgery with succinylcholine, a patient complains of diffuse muscle aches. The nurse explains this is because:
options: The drug's initial depolarization causes fasciculations
Malignant hyperthermia always causes mild muscle aches
The drug blocked Nm receptors without depolarizing them
practice.rationale: Sux is an Nm agonist — the initial depolarization causes brief fasciculations and postoperative muscle pain. Nondepolarizers don't depolarize, so they don't cause this.

practice.stem: A patient's BP rises from 84/50 to 150/92 on phenylephrine, and HR falls from 88 to 58. The best explanation is:
practice.rationale: Phenylephrine is a pure α₁ agonist: vasoconstriction raises BP, and the baroreceptor reflex slows the heart to compensate. It has no β₁-blocking or muscarinic action.

practice.stem: A patient has used albuterol many times a day for a week. Which lab value is most important to check?
options: Serum potassium, which may be low
Serum potassium, which may be high
practice.rationale: β₂ stimulation activates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and shifts K⁺ into cells → hypokalemia, especially with higher systemic exposure. Hyperkalemia is the succinylcholine problem.

practice.stem: A patient taking clonidine says, "I feel dizzy, so I'm just going to stop it." The best response is:
options: "Don't stop suddenly — your BP can rebound high."
"Take a double dose tomorrow to make up for it."
"You can stop it whenever you like if you feel dizzy."
"Stopping it will make your blood pressure drop further."
practice.rationale: MAJOR SAFETY ISSUE: abrupt discontinuation → rebound sympathetic activity → severe hypertension, tachycardia, headache. It should be tapered; teach slow position changes for the dizziness.

practice.stem: A patient is starting prazosin for hypertension. Which instruction addresses its major safety concern?
options: Stop the drug if your nose feels stuffy
Take the first dose with breakfast so you can watch for side effects
Take the first dose at bedtime and rise slowly
Expect your heart rate to slow on the first dose
practice.rationale: First-dose effect: significant orthostatic hypotension/syncope after the initial dose, so the first dose is commonly given at bedtime with fall precautions. Reflex tachycardia, not bradycardia, may occur.

practice.stem: A patient with asthma needs a β-blocker. Which drug raises the greatest concern for bronchoconstriction?
practice.rationale: Propranolol blocks β₂, so its bronchoconstriction concern is "higher" (slide 72). Metoprolol's β₁ selectivity lowers the concern (though it isn't absolute); prazosin and clonidine don't block β receptors.

practice.stem: Patient on propranolol for migraine prevention is wheezing. Albuterol is given. Predict:
options: Bronchodilation may be weaker than expected
Bronchodilation will be stronger than usual
No interaction — the drugs act on different receptors
practice.rationale: Both act at β₂: propranolol blocks it and "can oppose β₂ agonists such as albuterol." They share a receptor, so there is an interaction.

practice.stem: Patient with HR 38 receives atropine. HR rises to 92. Mechanism:
options: Direct β₁ stimulation of the heart
Increased ACh acting at the SA node
practice.rationale: "Atropine does not directly stimulate the heart, it removes the parasympathetic 'brake'." More ACh would slow the heart further; α₁ acts on vessels.

practice.stem: Bethanechol given. Predict sweating:
options: Increased — sweat glands use muscarinic receptors
Decreased — the drug is parasympathetic and sweating is sympathetic
No change — the PNS doesn't innervate sweat glands
practice.rationale: A muscarinic agonist "doesn't care" who normally controls the gland — it finds the muscarinic receptor, so sweating increases. That's the sweat-gland exception.

practice.stem: Patient on atropine works outdoors on a hot afternoon. Predict:
practice.rationale: Blocking muscarinic receptors on sweat glands ↓ sweating, so the patient can't cool off — teach to avoid overheating. Atropine causes tachycardia, not bradycardia.

practice.stem: Person with diabetes on metoprolol; blood glucose is low. Which sign is most likely still present?
practice.rationale: β-blockers blunt the adrenergic signs of hypoglycemia (tachycardia, tremor, anxiety), but sweating usually still occurs because sweat glands use ACh → muscarinic receptors.

practice.stem: Dobutamine started for low cardiac output in a patient with coronary disease. New chest pain. Why?
options: α₁ vasoconstriction of the coronary arteries
practice.rationale: Key concept: ↑ contractility = ↑ myocardial O₂ demand; angina is a listed adverse effect. Dobutamine is predominantly β₁, not α₁ or β₂, and it tends to raise HR, not lower it.

practice.stem: Norepinephrine infusing. IV site is swollen, cool and pale. Predict the risk:
practice.rationale: Norepinephrine is a powerful α₁ vasoconstrictor; extravasation causes local tissue injury/necrosis, which is why the IV site is monitored closely. This isn't a therapeutic effect.

practice.stem: Clonidine stopped abruptly 2 days ago. BP 190/110, HR 112, headache, nervous. Cause:
practice.rationale: Removing the α₂ "brake" suddenly → rebound sympathetic activity → severe hypertension, tachycardia, headache, nervousness. That's why clonidine is tapered.

practice.stem: Neostigmine given to reverse rocuronium. HR 52, copious secretions. Why?
options: The patient is developing malignant hyperthermia
Rocuronium is wearing off too fast
practice.rationale: AChE inhibitors raise ACh at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors, so bradycardia and secretions are muscarinic effects — the reason an antimuscarinic is commonly coadministered.

practice.stem: Myasthenia gravis patient takes pyridostigmine. Predict muscle strength and GI motility:
practice.rationale: More ACh is available at both Nm (better NMJ transmission in MG) and muscarinic receptors (↑ GI motility, cramping, diarrhea as adverse effects).

practice.stem: Tamsulosin started for BPH. Patient stands up quickly from bed. Predict:
practice.rationale: α₁A blockade relaxes prostate/bladder-neck smooth muscle, but dizziness and orthostatic hypotension are its main adverse effects — teach slow position changes. It improves urine flow and doesn't touch β₂.

practice.stem: Anaphylaxis: wheezing, BP 76/40. Epinephrine IM. Which receptor relieves the wheezing?
practice.rationale: β₂ → bronchodilation → improved airflow. α₁ raises BP and reduces mucosal edema; β₁ raises HR and contractility; α₂ isn't part of the anaphylaxis benefit.

clinical.title: Scenario 1 — Medical-surgical unit
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Post-op Day 2, 0800 67-year-old client 2 days after abdominal surgery. Has not voided for 9 hours; says she feels the urge but "nothing comes." Bladder scan shows a large volume of retained urine. History of kidney stones; reports new dull left flank pain since 0600. Mild asthma — uses a rescue inhaler a few times a year. Bowel sounds present in all quadrants, passing flatus. Incision clean and dry. Vital Signs — T 37.1°C · HR 78 · BP 124/72 · RR 16 · SpO₂ 97% on room air Laboratory Results — Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · K⁺ 4.1 mEq/L Orders — Bethanechol PO · bladder scan after each void · vital signs every 4 h

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the chart before the first dose of bethanechol. Which findings require follow-up before the drug is given? Select all that apply.
options: Kidney stone history with new flank pain
questions.rationale: Bethanechol makes smooth muscle contract harder, so look for conditions where that is dangerous: urinary or GI obstruction, significant bradycardia/hypotension, and conditions where bronchoconstriction could be dangerous. A stone with new flank pain could mean an obstruction; asthma is a bronchoconstriction risk. Bowel sounds with flatus argue against a GI obstruction, and her HR and BP are normal — those are reassuring, not red flags.

questions.stem: Why does the possibility of a stone matter so much for this drug?
options: The drug dissolves stones, which can cause sudden heavy bleeding
The drug relaxes the bladder wall, so a stone would worsen the retention
A stone blocks bladder muscarinic receptors, so the drug fails
Forcing the bladder to contract against a blocked outlet can rupture it
questions.rationale: "Before making the bladder contract harder, make sure it has a route for urine to get out." A stone stuck in the urethra plus a drug that squeezes the bladder can cause bladder rupture (the same logic applies to a bowel obstruction). Bethanechol contracts, not relaxes, the detrusor, and it has no effect on stones or receptor blockade.

questions.stem: What is the nurse's priority action at this time?
options: Give the dose now, since a full bladder is itself a danger
Give the dose with breakfast to lower the risk of nausea
Hold the dose and report the flank pain and stone history
Give the dose and repeat the bladder scan in about 1 hour
questions.rationale: Ruling out obstruction comes first — it's "usually not your responsibility, it's the prescriber's responsibility," but it's something the nurse should be thinking about, so she holds and reports. Giving it now ignores a possible obstruction; bethanechol is given on an empty stomach, not with a meal.

questions.stem: Day 2, 1000. Ultrasound shows no obstruction; the provider confirms the bethanechol order. Which nursing actions should the nurse plan? Select all that apply.
options: Monitor respiratory status because of her asthma
Give it on an empty stomach
Give it with a full meal to protect the stomach
Track urine output and bladder emptying
questions.rationale: Nursing implications on the slide: monitor BP and HR, urinary output/bladder emptying, abdominal symptoms, and respiratory status in at-risk patients. It's often given on an empty stomach to reduce nausea/vomiting. A meal is the wrong direction, and fluid restriction isn't part of the plan.

questions.stem: Day 2, 1130. One hour after the dose: HR 46, BP 92/54, expiratory wheezes, heavy sweating, abdominal cramping and two loose stools. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give the next bethanechol dose early to empty the bladder
Anticipate neostigmine to restore bladder muscle tone
Report the findings and anticipate an order for atropine
Anticipate phenylephrine to bring the HR back up
questions.rationale: Bradycardia, bronchoconstriction, sweating, cramping and diarrhea = too much muscarinic stimulation. "If we have a severe cholinergic effect… we can give the medication atropine." More bethanechol or neostigmine adds cholinergic activity; phenylephrine raises BP and can slow the heart further (reflex bradycardia).

questions.stem: Day 2, 1400. Atropine was given at 1145. Which findings show that the plan is working? Select all that apply.
options: Voided 450 mL; small residual on bladder scan
questions.rationale: HR back up, no bronchoconstriction or sweating, and a good void with a small residual means the retention was treated and the cholinergic excess reversed. Urinary urgency is a listed bethanechol adverse effect ("sometimes we can go too far"), and persistent bradycardia with dizziness needs follow-up.

clinical.title: Scenario 2 — Emergency department → medical unit
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 0930 81-year-old client brought in by his daughter after nearly fainting at home; dizzy, pale and cool. History: benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), hypertension, and an eye doctor once told him he has narrow-angle glaucoma. Home medications include two drugs with anticholinergic properties — one prescribed, one an OTC sleep aid. Lives alone and walks daily. Vital Signs — HR 38 · BP 82/48 · RR 18 · SpO₂ 95% · T 36.9°C Laboratory Results — K⁺ 4.2 mEq/L · glucose 102 mg/dL Orders — Atropine IV · continuous cardiac monitoring · admit to medical unit

questions.stem: Which findings increase this client's risk of adverse effects from atropine? Select all that apply.
options: Two home drugs with anticholinergic properties
questions.rationale: Antimuscarinic effects can worsen narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention/BPH. Older adults are "much more sensitive to anticholinergic drugs," and other drugs with anticholinergic properties add to the risk. Hypertension and daily walks aren't on the precaution list.

questions.stem: How will atropine raise this client's heart rate?
options: It blocks muscarinic receptors and removes the brake
It constricts vessels via α₁ so a reflex speeds the heart
It directly stimulates β₁ receptors in the heart
It slows the breakdown of acetylcholine at the SA node
questions.rationale: "We're not directly stimulating the heart, but we're removing the brake." Muscarinic activity normally slows the heart; blocking it lets HR rise. β₁ stimulation is a different (adrenergic) mechanism; slowing ACh breakdown would slow the heart; α₁ vasoconstriction triggers reflex bradycardia.

questions.stem: Day 2, 1600. HR has stayed 70–80 since one dose of atropine; his home medications were resumed. Staff now report he is newly confused and agitated, has had no bowel movement in 3 days, his bladder is distended, his mouth is very dry, and T is 38.1°C after an afternoon in a sunny window seat. The client is most likely experiencing:
options: Expected changes of aging that need no follow-up
Additive anticholinergic effects of his drugs
Reflex bradycardia now that his BP is higher
questions.rationale: Confusion, constipation, retention, dry mouth and overheating (↓ sweating → heat intolerance) are all anticholinergic effects, stacked by cumulative burden in an older adult. Cholinergic toxicity would look opposite (SLUDGE, bradycardia). These are drug effects, not normal aging, and his HR is normal.

questions.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in his plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Avoid overheating; encourage fluids unless contraindicated
Restrict fluids to limit bladder distention
Review prescription and OTC drugs for anticholinergic effects
Give atropine to settle the agitation
questions.rationale: Straight from the nursing implications: monitor bowel/bladder, assess cognition, avoid overheating, encourage hydration when not contraindicated, provide oral care, and review Rx and OTC drugs for anticholinergic effects. Atropine would add to the burden, and restricting fluids works against the hydration goal.

questions.stem: At bedtime the client asks for his usual OTC sleep aid, which has anticholinergic properties. What should the nurse do?
options: Give it with a large glass of water to prevent dry mouth
Give it, since OTC products don't add to the effects of prescription drugs
Hold it and ask the provider to review his anticholinergic drugs
Give it and request atropine if the confusion worsens
questions.rationale: Anticholinergic drugs are on the Beers list — drugs with a higher rate of adverse reactions in adults over 65. OTC drugs count toward the cumulative burden, which is why the slide says to review prescription and OTC medications. Water doesn't fix the confusion or retention; atropine adds more of the same effect.

questions.stem: Day 3, 1000. The provider stopped the sleep aid and changed his prescribed anticholinergic drug. Which findings show the plan is working? Select all that apply.
options: Blurred vision and sensitivity to light
questions.rationale: Clear thinking, bowel and bladder function back and a normal temperature show the anticholinergic load is easing. Blurred vision/photophobia and tachycardia are ongoing anticholinergic effects (atropine = "dry + fast + retention") — they need follow-up.

clinical.title: Scenario 3 — Emergency department
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1900 41-year-old client with myasthenia gravis takes pyridostigmine. She took extra doses this week because her eyelids were drooping. Now drooling, eyes watering, urinating frequently, diarrhea, vomited 3 times, abdominal cramping. Visible twitching in the arms and face. Pupils small. Allergic to penicillin (rash). Works as a teacher. Vital Signs — HR 50 · BP 98/60 · RR 22 · SpO₂ 93% · T 37.0°C · lungs: wheezes with copious secretions Laboratory Results — Glucose 96 mg/dL · K⁺ 3.9 mEq/L Orders — Atropine IV · continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry · respiratory assessment every 15 min

questions.stem: Which findings suggest excessive cholinergic activity? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: SLUDGE — Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis — plus miosis, bradycardia, bronchospasm and secretions. The drooping eyelids were her myasthenia (the reason she took extra doses), not drug excess; the allergy is unrelated.

questions.stem: Why did the extra doses of pyridostigmine produce these findings?
options: Her antibodies have now started destroying muscarinic receptors too
Pyridostigmine blocks muscarinic receptors, so the effects rebounded
Blocking AChE let ACh build up at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors
Pyridostigmine directly activates muscarinic receptors, like bethanechol
questions.rationale: AChE inhibitors don't activate receptors themselves — they slow ACh breakdown so it can "persist and hang out longer" at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Direct activation is bethanechol; blocking muscarinic receptors is atropine. MG destroys Nm receptors at the NMJ.

questions.stem: Day 1, 2015. The twitching is now followed by increasing weakness; she can barely lift her head. RR 26, SpO₂ 91%. What is the nurse's priority concern?
options: Worsening myasthenia from too little drug
Dehydration from all of the vomiting and diarrhea
Overheating because she has stopped sweating
questions.rationale: Excess nicotinic stimulation runs fasciculations → weakness → paralysis. "If we start seeing any weird muscle twitching in a patient who's taking some of these medications, it may mean that we've given them too much." With MG, monitor muscle strength and respiratory function — breathing comes first. This is too much drug, not too little.

questions.stem: Which interventions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Atropine for the dangerous muscarinic effects
Another dose of pyridostigmine for the weakness
Bethanechol to control the urinary frequency
questions.rationale: Atropine is used to treat cholinergic toxicity; nursing implications are HR/BP, respiratory status and secretions, and (with MG) muscle strength and respiratory function. More pyridostigmine or bethanechol would add cholinergic activity.

questions.stem: Day 1, 2030. Atropine has been given. Which assessment should the nurse repeat most closely now?
options: Pupil size and reaction to light
Bowel sounds in all four abdominal quadrants
questions.rationale: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors, so it treats the SLUDGE effects; the weakness comes from nicotinic excess at the NMJ. With MG the slide's focus is muscle strength and respiratory function. Glucose, bowel sounds and pupils don't threaten her airway.

questions.stem: Day 1, 2230. Which findings show the treatment is working? Select all that apply.
options: Twitching continues; cannot lift her head
No vomiting or diarrhea in the last hour
questions.rationale: Fewer secretions, a normal HR and settled GI symptoms show the muscarinic excess is controlled. Ongoing fasciculations with weakness and worsening oxygenation mean the nicotinic effects are progressing — report immediately.

clinical.title: Scenario 4 — Medical ICU
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1100 58-year-old client with severe respiratory failure, intubated and mechanically ventilated, keeps fighting the ventilator. The provider starts a rocuronium infusion. He is also being treated for pneumonia with gentamicin IV, and magnesium sulfate IV is ordered for a low magnesium level. Eyes partly open. Wife at the bedside. Vital Signs — T 38.2°C · HR 96 · BP 118/70 · ventilator rate 18 · SpO₂ 92% Laboratory Results — WBC 15,000/mm³ · Mg 1.4 mg/dL (low) · K⁺ 4.0 mEq/L Orders — Rocuronium infusion · gentamicin IV · magnesium sulfate IV · peripheral nerve stimulation (train-of-four)

questions.stem: Which items on the chart could increase or prolong the rocuronium blockade? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Slide 41 interactions: blockade may be increased or prolonged by certain general anesthetics, aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin) and magnesium. The WBC and fever are about his pneumonia; normal K⁺ and age aren't on the list.

questions.stem: Day 1, 1300. He now lies completely still with no purposeful movement. His wife asks, "He looks peaceful — does that mean he's asleep and comfortable?" Which statement is accurate?
options: He is paralyzed but may still be awake and able to feel pain
The paralytic treats pain, so analgesia can stop
Lying this still shows his sedation dose is enough
The paralytic also keeps him asleep, so he can't feel pain
questions.rationale: PARALYSIS ≠ SEDATION ≠ ANALGESIA — blockers give no unconsciousness, sedation or pain relief, so patients need additional medications. "There have been horror stories of people who have undergone surgery completely paralyzed but were not sedated." Stillness tells you nothing about sedation or pain.

questions.stem: While the rocuronium infusion runs, which need is the nurse's highest priority?
options: Range-of-motion exercises every 2 h to prevent stiffness
Ventilation, because his breathing muscles are paralyzed
Hourly pupil checks to track the paralysis
Hourly pain scores on a 0–10 scale he points to
questions.rationale: Blockers paralyze the respiratory muscles too — "it will kill the patient if you don't have a way to make them breathe," so ventilatory support must be immediately available. He can't point to a pain scale while paralyzed, and depth of blockade is checked with peripheral nerve stimulation, not pupils.

questions.stem: Which actions belong in his plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Stop ventilatory support as soon as the infusion ends
Ensure sedation and analgesia are given
Eye care to protect the corneas
Monitor blockade depth with peripheral nerve stimulation
Hold analgesia since he shows no signs of pain
questions.rationale: A paralyzed patient can't blink or shift his weight — "their cornea drying out… pressure ulcers" — so eye, skin and positioning care, plus sedation/analgesia and monitoring of blockade depth (train-of-four). He can't show pain, and recovery must be verified before respiratory support stops.

questions.stem: Day 4, 0900. The infusion is stopped and neostigmine is given with an antimuscarinic to reverse the blockade. Before ventilatory support is discontinued, the nurse must:
options: Confirm that his heart rate is below 60/min
Verify that he has adequate neuromuscular recovery
Give a second neostigmine dose to finish reversal
Make sure sedation has been off for 24 hours
questions.rationale: "Make sure that the patient can breathe before we pull that tube out." Neostigmine is an AChE inhibitor: ↓ ACh breakdown → ↑ ACh at the NMJ → ACh competes more effectively with the blocker for Nm receptors. Bradycardia is a muscarinic adverse effect, not a goal.

questions.stem: Day 4, 0930. Which findings after neostigmine need follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Moves all four limbs on command
questions.rationale: More ACh reaches muscarinic receptors too, so neostigmine's high-yield safety concern is muscarinic effects — bradycardia, secretions, bronchoconstriction (that's why an antimuscarinic is commonly coadministered). Purposeful movement, spontaneous breathing and nerve-stimulation recovery show the blockade is reversing.

clinical.title: Scenario 5 — Pre-op holding → operating room
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 0700 34-year-old client with major burns 2 weeks ago, past the acute phase, on bed rest for most of the last 10 days. Scheduled for surgical debridement under general anesthesia with a volatile inhaled anesthetic; the anesthesia plan lists succinylcholine for intubation. During the pre-op interview he says his uncle "had a bad reaction to anesthesia once — he got really hot." NPO since midnight. Nonsmoker. Vital Signs — T 37.2°C · HR 98 · BP 128/78 · RR 18 · SpO₂ 97% Laboratory Results — K⁺ 4.6 mEq/L · Hgb 11.8 g/dL · glucose 110 mg/dL Orders — General anesthesia · pre-op checklist · dantrolene available in the OR

questions.stem: Which findings are risk factors for serious complications of succinylcholine? Select all that apply.
options: Bed rest for most of 10 days
questions.rationale: Hyperkalemia risk: major burns after the acute phase, crush injury/trauma, spinal cord injury, denervation, prolonged immobilization, certain neuromuscular disorders. A personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia means avoid or use extreme caution — that's why you're asked whether "anyone in your family ever had a negative reaction to anesthesia." Being NPO is routine, and the HR and Hgb aren't risk factors.

questions.stem: Why is succinylcholine especially dangerous for this client's burns?
options: Burns drain potassium, so the drug causes a severe hypokalemia
Burned skin soaks up the drug and causes local tissue necrosis
Burned muscle breaks the drug down too quickly for it to paralyze
Extra ACh receptors let more K⁺ leave muscle on depolarization
questions.rationale: Burns upregulate extrajunctional ACh receptors → more channels open during depolarization → greater K⁺ efflux → severe hyperkalemia → life-threatening dysrhythmias. "Their bodies are a little bit more primed." Hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia, is the risk.

questions.stem: Day 1, 0920. Anesthesia used rocuronium instead. Twenty minutes into surgery with the volatile anesthetic, end-tidal CO₂ is rising rapidly and his jaw and limbs are rigid. HR 132. T 37.8°C. The client is most likely experiencing:
options: Malignant hyperthermia from the volatile anesthetic
Cholinergic toxicity from excess ACh at the NMJ
Hyperkalemia from succinylcholine given at intubation
questions.rationale: Certain volatile inhaled anesthetics can trigger MH on their own in susceptible people. Rising EtCO₂ + rigidity are the early clues; "it's like carbon dioxide that is often the first sign," and hyperthermia may be late, so a near-normal temperature doesn't rule it out. He never got succinylcholine, and a blocker causes flaccid, not rigid, muscles.

questions.stem: Which interventions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Monitor cardiovascular and respiratory status, K⁺ and temperature
Give succinylcholine to relax the rigid muscles
Wait until the temperature is above 40°C to treat
questions.rationale: Treatment: stop triggering agents + supportive management ("buckets of ice," cooling blankets) + dantrolene, the antidote. Monitor CV/respiratory status, K⁺ and temperature. Waiting for fever misses the window — hyperthermia is late; succinylcholine is itself a trigger.

questions.stem: Place the team's malignant hyperthermia actions in priority order.
options: Keep monitoring cardiovascular and respiratory status
Recognize the early signs: rising end-tidal CO₂ and rigidity
Give dantrolene and start supportive cooling
questions.rationale: Recognize early signs → stop the trigger → dantrolene (which must be rapidly available wherever triggers are used) with cooling → ongoing CV/respiratory monitoring.

questions.stem: Day 1, 1100. Which findings show treatment is working? Select all that apply.
options: K⁺ rising above the reference range
questions.rationale: MH = abnormal Ca²⁺ release → sustained muscle activity and hypermetabolism → ↑ CO₂, rigidity, tachycardia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, rising temperature. Falling CO₂, relaxed muscles, slower HR and a normal temperature mean it's reversing; rising K⁺ or temperature means it isn't.

clinical.title: Scenario 6 — Emergency department
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1915 19-year-old college student with a known peanut allergy ate a cookie containing peanuts 15 minutes ago. Hives on the chest and arms, swollen lips, wheezing and a hoarse voice. She carries an epinephrine autoinjector but didn't use it. Reports palpitations "sometimes when I drink a lot of coffee." Takes no daily medications. Vital Signs — BP 78/40 · HR 128 · RR 28 · SpO₂ 90% · T 36.8°C Laboratory Results — Glucose 98 mg/dL Orders — Epinephrine IM now · continuous cardiac monitoring · pulse oximetry

questions.stem: Which findings show the reaction is compromising her airway and breathing? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis causes bronchoconstriction + airway edema → impaired ventilation (wheezing, hoarseness, lip/mucosal swelling, falling SpO₂). Hives are skin findings, and the palpitations history doesn't describe her airway.

questions.stem: Put these events in order, from exposure to epinephrine's effect.
options: Epinephrine α₁ vasoconstriction raises BP and reduces mucosal edema
questions.rationale: Mediator release → vasodilation + ↑ permeability → hypotension + tissue edema; epinephrine's α₁ effect reverses it (↑ BP, ↓ mucosal edema).

questions.stem: Her HR is 128 and she mentions palpitations with coffee. What is the nurse's priority?
options: Hold the epinephrine until her HR is below 100
Give it only if her systolic BP falls below 70
Give the epinephrine without any delay
Ask for phenylephrine to avoid β₁ stimulation
questions.rationale: "In a life-threatening emergency such as anaphylaxis, there is no absolute contraindication to appropriate epinephrine treatment." Caution with cardiovascular disease applies in other settings. Phenylephrine (α₁ only) wouldn't open her airways, and waiting lets the airway close.

questions.stem: Which effects of epinephrine will help this client? Select all that apply.
options: β₁ increases heart rate and contractility
α₁ vasoconstriction raises BP and reduces mucosal edema
questions.rationale: Epinephrine hits everything — α₁, β₁, β₂ — the "ideal receptor profile for anaphylaxis." Muscarinic stimulation causes bronchoconstriction, and α₂ activation decreases NE release.

questions.stem: How should the nurse give the epinephrine?
options: As a slow IV push over 1 minute
IM into the deltoid muscle of the arm
questions.rationale: Slide 54 nursing implication: for anaphylaxis, IM administration in the anterolateral thigh.

questions.stem: Day 1, 2000. Which findings need follow-up? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: BP, oxygenation, airway swelling and voice show the drug is working. Chest pain (angina), tachycardia and dysrhythmias are adverse effects of excessive adrenergic stimulation — monitor HR, BP, rhythm and response, and report them.

clinical.title: Scenario 7 — Medical ICU
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1000 66-year-old client with septic shock from pneumonia remains hypotensive. IV fluids are running. A norepinephrine (Levophed) infusion is started through a peripheral IV in the left forearm and titrated to a prescribed BP target. History: type 2 diabetes. Vital Signs — BP 78/42 · HR 118 · T 38.9°C · RR 24 · SpO₂ 94% · urine output 15 mL/h Laboratory Results — WBC 18,000/mm³ · glucose 168 mg/dL Orders — Norepinephrine infusion titrated to BP target · IV fluids · continuous BP and ECG monitoring · hourly urine output

questions.stem: Day 1, 1200. Two hours into the infusion: IV site swollen, cool and pale; fingers cool and dusky; BP 146/88 (above the prescribed target); urine output 35 mL/h; HR 102; T 38.4°C. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: IV site swollen, cool and pale
questions.rationale: Norepinephrine's adverse effects: excessive hypertension, decreased peripheral perfusion with excessive vasoconstriction, ischemia, extravasation → local tissue injury. Rising urine output and a falling HR are signs of improvement; the temperature is part of her sepsis, not the drug.

questions.stem: The cool, dusky fingers with a BP above target are most consistent with:
options: Hypovolemia that the drug has now corrected
An expected sign that the drug is working
questions.rationale: Strong α₁ stimulation → peripheral vasoconstriction. Overshoot the target and perfusion to the fingers drops (ischemia); assess perfusion and titrate to the prescribed target. Norepinephrine has no β₂ activity, and vasoconstriction never replaces volume.

questions.stem: Which complication is the swollen, cool, pale IV site most likely signaling?
options: Hypokalemia as the drug shifts K⁺ into cells
Reflex bradycardia at the infusion site
questions.rationale: Extravasation → local tissue injury/necrosis — that's why the slide says to monitor the IV site closely. Reflex bradycardia is a heart-rate response (phenylephrine); K⁺ shifting into cells is a β₂ (albuterol) effect.

questions.stem: Which actions belong in her plan while she is on norepinephrine? Select all that apply.
options: Titrate to the prescribed hemodynamic target
Continuous BP and cardiac rhythm monitoring
Stop IV fluids since the drug restores volume
Titrate to the highest BP she can tolerate
questions.rationale: Nursing implications: continuous BP/hemodynamic and rhythm monitoring, peripheral perfusion, IV site, and titration to the prescribed target. Vasoconstriction does not replace circulating volume, and higher isn't better — excess causes ischemia.

questions.stem: Day 1, 1600. BP is back at target. A resident asks whether the IV fluids can be stopped because the norepinephrine is "holding the pressure." The nurse's best response is:
options: "Volume still has to be addressed — the drug doesn't replace it."
"Yes — norepinephrine expands her circulating blood volume."
"No — the fluids are needed to dilute the drug and protect the vein."
"Yes — fluids given with a vasopressor will cause hypertension."
questions.rationale: Slide 55 precaution: hypovolemia should be recognized and addressed, because vasoconstriction does not replace adequate circulating volume. Norepinephrine tightens the vessels; it doesn't add volume.

questions.stem: Day 2, 1000. She was switched to phenylephrine. BP 132/80 (at target), HR fell from 110 to 52; she reports dizziness. Urine output 50 mL/h. Which findings need follow-up? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Phenylephrine is pure α₁: BP rises and the baroreceptors slow the heart — reflex bradycardia ("we've given them a pressure medication… let's compensate by slowing down the heart rate"). Headache is also a listed adverse effect. BP at target, good urine output and warm fingers show the plan is working.

clinical.title: Scenario 8 — Cardiac step-down unit
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1200 70-year-old client with heart failure and coronary artery disease admitted with signs of low cardiac output: cool extremities, low urine output, fatigue. History of episodes of atrial fibrillation. Took his home metoprolol this morning. A dobutamine infusion is started. Vital Signs — HR 88 · BP 92/58 · RR 20 · SpO₂ 94% · T 36.7°C Laboratory Results — K⁺ 4.3 mEq/L · creatinine 1.3 mg/dL Orders — Dobutamine infusion · continuous ECG and BP monitoring · strict intake and output

questions.stem: Which findings could affect how well dobutamine works or how safely it can be given? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Use dobutamine cautiously with dysrhythmias and ischemic heart disease, and β-blockers may reduce its β₁-mediated effects — both drugs act at β₁. The other findings aren't on the list.

questions.stem: What is the goal of the dobutamine infusion?
options: Vasoconstriction that raises systemic vascular resistance
Slowing the heart rate so the heart can rest
questions.rationale: Dobutamine is predominantly β₁: ↑ myocardial contractility → ↑ SV → ↑ CO (it may also raise HR). Vasoconstriction is α₁ (norepinephrine, phenylephrine); bronchodilation is β₂ (albuterol).

questions.stem: Day 1, 1430. HR 118, BP 104/64; he reports chest pressure. The client is most likely experiencing:
options: An expected and harmless effect of the dobutamine
Reflex bradycardia as his blood pressure rises
Increased myocardial oxygen demand from the drug
questions.rationale: Key concept: ↑ contractility = ↑ myocardial O₂ demand. Tachycardia and angina are listed adverse effects — that's why caution is needed in ischemic heart disease. β₂ stimulation opens the airways; his HR went up, not down.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Increase the dobutamine to raise his output further
Report the chest pressure and HR to the provider
Give the next metoprolol dose early to boost dobutamine
questions.rationale: Nursing implications: continuous HR/rhythm monitoring, BP, response through perfusion/hemodynamic measures, and monitoring for chest pain and dysrhythmias. More dobutamine adds O₂ demand; a β-blocker reduces dobutamine's β₁ effects.

questions.stem: Day 4, 0800. Dobutamine was weaned; the provider orders carvedilol in place of metoprolol. Before the first dose: HR 50, BP 86/52, client dizzy when sitting up. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the dose and recheck vital signs next shift
Give half now and the rest once he feels better
Hold the dose and report his HR and BP findings
Give the dose and keep him flat in bed today
questions.rationale: Carvedilol causes bradycardia, hypotension and orthostatic hypotension; use cautiously with bradycardia and in patients vulnerable to hypotension. Monitor HR and BP and report symptomatic bradycardia/hypotension rather than giving a drug that will lower both further.

questions.stem: Day 5. Discharge teaching on carvedilol. Which statements show the client understood? Select all that apply.
options: "I'll check my pulse and blood pressure as I was shown."
"I won't stop it suddenly, even if I feel fine."
"I'll report it if my heart failure symptoms get worse."
"I'll get up slowly if I feel dizzy."
"I'll skip a dose on days that I feel dizzy."
"It only acts on my heart, so it can't affect my breathing."
questions.rationale: Carvedilol blocks β₁ + β₂ + α₁: α₁ blockade → vasodilation → more orthostatic hypotension than metoprolol, so rise slowly. Don't stop abruptly; watch for worsening HF when therapy starts or is titrated; monitor HR and BP. It blocks β₂ too (bronchospasm risk), and skipping doses is a version of stopping abruptly.

clinical.title: Scenario 9 — Primary care clinic
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Visit 1, 0900 52-year-old client with hypertension on clonidine, asthma treated with an albuterol rescue inhaler, and type 1 diabetes on insulin. Ran out of clonidine 2 days ago. Reports a pounding headache and feeling "jittery." Has used albuterol about 8 times a day this week; hands have a fine tremor. Up to date on vaccines. Vital Signs — BP 188/108 · HR 110 · RR 20 · SpO₂ 96% · T 36.8°C Laboratory Results — K⁺ 3.3 mEq/L (low) · glucose 142 mg/dL Orders — Provider to see client · renew clonidine

questions.stem: Which findings need follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: BP 188/108 two days after running out of clonidine
Albuterol about 8 times a day this week
questions.rationale: Stopping clonidine suddenly can cause severe hypertension. Frequent need for rescue medication may indicate inadequate disease control, and β₂ stimulation shifts K⁺ into cells (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase), so heavy albuterol use can lower serum K⁺. Normal SpO₂ and temperature and her vaccines aren't concerns.

questions.stem: Her BP, HR, headache and jitteriness are most consistent with:
options: Rebound sympathetic activity after stopping clonidine
α₁ blockade causing a reflex rise in BP
β₂ stimulation from albuterol constricting vessels
Clonidine overdose from doses taken too close together
questions.rationale: Sudden discontinuation → rebound sympathetic activity → severe hypertension, tachycardia, headache, nervousness. Clonidine excess would lower BP and HR. α₁ blockade lowers BP (reflex tachycardia, not hypertension). Albuterol can cause tachycardia and tremor, but not this BP.

questions.stem: Which explanation of her albuterol use is the priority for the provider to address?
options: The tremor shows albuterol has stopped working
Albuterol is the main cause of her BP of 188/108
Her asthma is not adequately controlled
Albuterol is a maintenance drug, so this is expected
questions.rationale: Slide 58: reinforce the difference between rescue and maintenance therapy; frequent need for rescue medication may indicate inadequate disease control. Tremor is an expected albuterol adverse effect, not a sign it stopped working.

questions.stem: Visit 2, two weeks later. Clonidine was restarted. The provider is considering adding a β-blocker. Which points should the nurse anticipate raising? Select all that apply.
options: Propranolol is a higher bronchospasm concern than metoprolol
Metoprolol blocks β₂ as strongly as propranolol
Metoprolol's β₁ selectivity is not absolute
β-blockers can mask a racing heart and tremor in hypoglycemia
questions.rationale: Propranolol blocks β₁ + β₂ ("higher" concern); metoprolol is β₁-preferring ("lower"), but selectivity isn't absolute. β-blockers can oppose β₂ agonists. They blunt tachycardia, tremor and anxiety in hypoglycemia — but sweating usually still occurs, because sweat glands use ACh → muscarinic receptors.

questions.stem: Which teaching about clonidine is the nurse's priority?
options: Stop it once the new β-blocker is started
Take it only on days your home BP reading is high
Skip a dose whenever it makes you drowsy
Never stop it suddenly; taper only as directed
questions.rationale: MAJOR SAFETY ISSUE: do not stop abruptly — taper rather than discontinue, and reinforce adherence. Skipping or stopping doses is exactly what caused her rebound hypertension. Sedation is expected; warn about it rather than skipping doses.

questions.stem: Visit 3. She now takes metoprolol and clonidine. Which statements show she understood the teaching? Select all that apply.
options: "If I'm sweaty, I'll check my sugar even if my heart isn't racing."
"I'll call if I need my albuterol more often."
"If I feel sleepy I can skip my clonidine."
"I'll change positions slowly if I feel dizzy."
"I won't stop metoprolol on my own."
"A racing heart will still warn me that my sugar is low."
questions.rationale: β-blockers can mask some hypoglycemia signs — tachycardia, tremor, anxiety are blunted, but sweating usually still occurs. Don't abruptly stop chronic β-blocker therapy; frequent rescue use may mean poor control; rise slowly with clonidine. A racing heart is exactly the warning that gets masked, and skipping clonidine risks rebound.

clinical.title: Scenario 10 — Rapid rounds
clinical.setting: Clinic, procedure unit and ED · one question each
clinical.text: Six clients, one question each. Use the receptor, then predict the drug effect.

questions.stem: A client is starting prazosin for hypertension. When should the first dose be taken?
options: First thing in the morning, before breakfast
With the largest meal of the day
Only when a home BP reading is high
questions.rationale: First-dose effect: significant orthostatic hypotension/syncope can follow the first dose (or a big dose increase), so the initial dose is commonly given at bedtime. Teach to rise slowly; fall precautions when symptomatic.

questions.stem: A man with BPH starting tamsulosin asks, "Will this shrink my prostate?" The nurse's best answer:
options: "Yes — it shrinks the prostate within a week."
"No — it eases urine flow but doesn't shrink it."
"Yes — it shrinks the gland by blocking β₂ receptors."
"No — it only lowers your blood pressure."
questions.rationale: α₁A blockade relaxes smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck → improved urine flow. Teach that it improves flow but does not eliminate the underlying prostate enlargement. Dizziness/orthostasis are its main adverse effects.

questions.stem: Five days after botulinum toxin injections for chronic migraine, a client reports trouble swallowing, generalized weakness and shortness of breath. These findings suggest:
options: Rare systemic spread of the injected toxin
An expected local effect needing no follow-up
Malignant hyperthermia triggered by the toxin
questions.rationale: Adverse effects are usually excess local weakness, but rare systemic spread can cause generalized weakness, dysphagia and respiratory compromise — "the absolute worst case scenario." Watch swallowing, breathing and muscle weakness; other drugs that impair neuromuscular transmission may add to it.

questions.stem: Why does botulinum toxin reduce excessive underarm sweating (hyperhidrosis)?
options: It blocks the α₁ receptors on sweat glands
Sweat glands are run by the parasympathetic system
It boosts norepinephrine release in the skin
Sweat glands run on ACh at muscarinic receptors
questions.rationale: Botulinum toxin prevents presynaptic ACh release. "Even though sweating is sympathetic, it is under the control of muscarinic" receptors — sympathetic nerves release ACh at sweat glands — so cutting ACh release stops the sweating.

questions.stem: In the ED, the team chooses succinylcholine for an emergency intubation. What makes it the usual choice here?
options: It sedates the client as well as paralyzing them
It leaves the breathing muscles working normally
questions.rationale: It's used when rapid airway control/intubation is needed — "this one is a lot faster, so especially in emergency situations in ER setting." It's an Nm agonist that causes persistent depolarization → flaccid paralysis, including the respiratory muscles, and gives no sedation. Neostigmine reverses nondepolarizing blockers.

questions.stem: A client treated for anaphylaxis is going home with an epinephrine autoinjector. Which teaching is most important?
options: Inject it into a vein if symptoms are severe or worsening
No follow-up is needed once the autoinjector is used
Use it only if the hives spread down to the legs as well
Correct use, then emergency evaluation after any use
questions.rationale: Slide 54: teach patients prescribed autoinjectors correct use and the need for emergency evaluation after administration. The route for anaphylaxis is IM in the anterolateral thigh, never a vein.

qa.q: Piloerection — which is the fancy name for…?
qa.a: Goosebumps (the class answered) — "you get to look bigger."

qa.q: (student asked) Are Nn and Nm both ion channels?
qa.a: Yes — both ion channels: we want a fast muscle response and fast transfer between neurons. Follow-ups weren't audible; she added that muscarinic receptors are the ones at the parasympathetic target organs, and the second diagram shows the same thing.

qa.q: If an α₁ agonist causes vasoconstriction, what would happen if we gave an α₁ antagonist?
qa.a: Vasodilation → ↓ BP — "good."

qa.q: If an α₁ agonist causes contraction of the prostate and bladder smooth muscle, what would happen if we gave an α₁ antagonist?
qa.a: Relaxation → improved urine flow. "Opposite side of the coin for almost everything except for sweat."

qa.q: (student asked) [mostly inaudible — about epinephrine vs norepinephrine at these receptors]
qa.a: They bind with different strengths, "a little beyond where I need you to be" — learn the receptor first, then match drugs to it.

qa.q: (student asked) [about what α₂ activation does / is used for]
qa.a: ↓ BP — it tells NE-releasing cells to "slow down a little"; also an adjunct for ADHD, PTSD and other off-label uses. Less heart rate, lower BP. (α₂ agonist — slide 19)

qa.q: (student asked) Does blocking just remove the brake — would it have the opposite effect?
qa.a: "Exactly." It depends on the drug, but vessels have no parasympathetic input, so pulling back the sympathetic → vasodilation.

qa.q: (student asked) So an α₂ antagonist would do the opposite?
qa.a: "Theoretically yes, but we don't have any drugs that do that." (slide 73: ↑ NE release*)

qa.q: Predict: stimulate α₁ → BP? β₁ → HR and contractility? β₂ → bronchi? Muscarinic → GI motility and bladder emptying?
qa.a: BP ↑ (from slide 18) · HR/contractility up · bronchi dilate (from slide 21) · muscarinic → "more, yes, more of that." (Her "predict the response" slide isn't in the posted deck — guided notes ¶40–47.)

qa.q: Now block them: α₁ → BP? β₁ → contractility? β₂ → bronchi? Muscarinic → GI and bladder?
qa.a: BP ↓ (from slide 18) · contractility down · bronchi constrict — "some good and bad things" · GI/bladder ↓ (from slide 73).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which neurotransmitter is released by all ANS preganglionic neurons?
qa.a: Acetylcholine — "it's always acetylcholine from that first neuron."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which receptor is found at the skeletal muscle neuromuscular junction?
qa.a: Nicotinic M (muscle).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Stimulation of α₁ receptors produces which effect?
qa.a: Vasoconstriction → ↑ BP (from slide 18) — α₁ is mainly on the vasculature, and "we manipulate them a lot when we're talking about blood pressure."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which effect is expected with β₁ receptor stimulation?
qa.a: ↑ HR and contractility — "one heart."

qa.q: (Kahoot) β₂ receptor stimulation produces which pulmonary effect?
qa.a: Bronchodilation — "if I'm running away from a bear… getting more air into my lungs."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Activation of α₂ receptors has which effect?
qa.a: ↓ NE release / ↓ sympathetic outflow (from slide 19) — "our negative feedback that keeps everything in check."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which response is caused by muscarinic receptor stimulation?
qa.a: Exact option not audible — "anything that the parasympathetic nervous system does" (from slide 22: e.g., ↓ HR, miosis, ↑ GI motility, bladder emptying, ↑ salivation).

qa.q: (Kahoot) A sudden medication-induced rise in blood pressure may trigger which response?
qa.a: Reflex bradycardia — reflex tachycardia is the opposite case, when BP falls.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Bethanechol is most appropriate for which condition?
qa.a: Nonobstructive urinary retention — "if we did have that block… we would risk potentially causing bladder rupture."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which finding is an expected adverse effect of bethanechol?
qa.a: Answer not audible — a cholinergic effect (from slide 30: bradycardia, hypotension, bronchoconstriction, diarrhea, salivation, sweating, urinary urgency). Her hint: the anticholinergic options (urinary retention, dry mouth) "are all going to be opposite."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Atropine produces which effect?
qa.a: Urinary retention.

qa.q: (Kahoot) How does pyridostigmine improve myasthenia gravis?
qa.a: It's an AChE inhibitor — blocks the breakdown of ACh, so more ACh at the neuromuscular junction.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which finding best suggests excessive cholinergic activity?
qa.a: A SLUDGE finding — "we got the S in there and the D."

qa.q: (student asked) Do nurses need someone to cosign for medications like these?
qa.a: Cosigning is mostly for wasting narcotics (e.g., a 5 mg dose from a 10 mg vial); she didn't think neuromuscular blockers require it. The Vanderbilt case involved multiple failures.
